title: The yo-yo is ancient
hook: A Greek cup painted around 440 BC shows a boy playing with a yo-yo.
peek: The yo-yo craze began in 1920s California, thanks to a Filipino immigrant called Pedro Flores. But the toy itself is far older. A painted Greek cup from around 440 BC shows a boy with one in his hand.
lede: Most people think of the yo-yo as a 20th-century fad, and the craze certainly was. The toy is much older. A painted drinking cup from ancient Athens, made around 440 BC and now in a museum, shows a boy spinning a disc on a string. Later, in 18th-century Europe, the toy was a fashion among adults, known in Britain as the bandalore.

bullets.text: Pedro Flores moved from the Philippines to the United States as a young man and opened a yo-yo factory in Santa Barbara, California, in 1928. He ran trick contests to show the toy off, and it spread fast.
Flores is often credited with looping the string around the axle instead of tying it. That lets the yo-yo keep spinning at the bottom of the string, called sleeping, which makes most tricks possible.

bullets.opening: Where the word yo-yo comes from
bullets.text: Flores used yo-yo, a word from his Philippine homeland. It is often said to mean 'come back', though language experts are not sure of that translation.

The businessman Donald F. Duncan bought Flores's company around 1930 and trademarked the name Yo-Yo. In 1965 a US court ruled the word had become an everyday name for the toy, so any maker could use it.
